research_domain_title: Community Enterprises, Cooperatives, Succession, Local Capital Access, and Local Prosperity Scores
note: Major dedicated architecture: reward measurable local prosperity outcomes associated with rooted ownership — not punish large businesses or prohibit outside investment. Foundational circulation claim is a design principle requiring empirical testing by place; do not invent local-multiplier percentages. Capital-access terms, tax incentives, and Local Prosperity Score weights require modeling. Legal drafting 0%. Architecture ≠ evidence that Community Investment Banks or Cooperative Development Centers already exist as described.

objective.text: Not to punish large businesses or prohibit outside investment, but to recognize that locally rooted ownership often keeps more wealth, decision-making, and civic engagement within the community — and to reward those outcomes rather than ownership structure alone.

foundational_principle.text: The closer ownership is to the community, the more likely wealth circulates within that community.
likely_effects_when_locally_owned: Profits are more likely to be reinvested locally
Owners are more likely to support schools, nonprofits, and civic organizations
Jobs are less likely to be relocated
Leadership is more accountable to the community
foundational_principle.design_rule: Reward these public benefits without preventing businesses from growing or competing nationally.
foundational_principle.evidence_note: Treat as a testable design principle — measure Local Prosperity Scores and multipliers rather than asserting universal automatic effects.

compact_language.text: Communities prosper when ownership is rooted where value is created. We will expand opportunities for family-owned businesses, employee-owned companies, agricultural cooperatives, consumer cooperatives, and locally controlled enterprises by improving access to capital, encouraging succession planning, supporting cooperative development, and recognizing businesses that reinvest in their communities. Our goal is not to favor one business model over another, but to reward enterprises that create lasting local wealth, strengthen civic life, and help communities thrive across generations.

market_alignment.text: This approach aligns with market principles while recognizing that ownership structure has public consequences. It encourages local and cooperative ownership because those models often produce broader community benefits, but it does so by rewarding measurable contributions to prosperity rather than excluding or penalizing other forms of business ownership.

community_enterprise_classification.title: Community Enterprise Classification
community_enterprise_classification.summary: Ownership categories that may qualify for different incentives. Businesses may qualify under more than one category.

categories.title: Community Cooperative
criteria: Owned by members such as farmers, consumers, or local businesses
Profits returned to members or reinvested

categories.title: Public Benefit Enterprise
criteria: Meets community investment, workforce, and environmental standards

local_prosperity_score.title: Local Prosperity Score
local_prosperity_score.summary: Incentives based on measurable contributions — not size alone. Higher scores unlock greater access to public incentives. Exact weights require modeling.

capital_access_advantage.title: Capital Access Advantage
capital_access_advantage.summary: Community Investment Banks or revolving loan funds prioritize businesses that strengthen the local economy under transparent eligibility standards.

tax_incentives.title: Tax Incentives for Keeping Ownership Local
tax_incentives.summary: Reward behaviors that build local prosperity rather than rewarding size alone. Encourage continuity and local commitment without restricting owners' choices.
examples: Selling to family members who continue operating locally
Reinvesting profits in expansion or workforce development

succession_protection.title: Succession Protection
succession_protection.summary: Help preserve productive businesses and local jobs when owners retire.

community_investment_priority.title: Community Investment Priority
community_investment_priority.summary: Public procurement may give appropriate weight to local economic impact, workforce development, community reinvestment, supplier diversity, reliability, price, and quality — recognizing full local value while remaining fair and competitive.

retirement_connection.title: Local Ownership Retirement Connection
retirement_connection.summary: Citizens may invest part of Community Prosperity Accounts in approved local enterprises; as enterprises succeed, participating residents share returns. Complements — does not replace — diversified retirement savings and fiduciary caps.

community_reinvestment_requirement.title: Community Reinvestment Requirement
community_reinvestment_requirement.summary: Businesses receiving substantial public incentives may commit to reinvesting a portion of profits into training, expansion, innovation, local philanthropy, community development, or environmental improvements — transparent and proportional to public support. Exact shares require modeling.

cooperative_development_initiative.title: Cooperative Development Initiative
cooperative_development_initiative.summary: Cooperative Development Centers make cooperative ownership a practical option rather than a niche concept.

local_economic_multipliers.title: Measuring Local Economic Multipliers
local_economic_multipliers.summary: Success measured by community impact as well as business revenue — without inventing unverified multiplier constants.

virtuous_cycle.title: The Virtuous Cycle
flow: Better schools, infrastructure, and public services

pillars.title: Reward Outcomes, Not Structure Alone
pillars.summary: Incentives follow measurable local prosperity contributions; outside investment and large firms remain free to compete.

pillars.title: Community Enterprise Classification
pillars.summary: Community, family, worker-coop, community-coop, and public-benefit categories — multi-qualification allowed.

pillars.title: Local Prosperity Score
pillars.summary: Score unlocks public incentives based on ownership, payroll, purchasing, wages, stewardship, and longevity.

pillars.title: Capital Access Advantage
pillars.summary: Patient community capital for expansion, succession, equipment, working capital, and disaster recovery.

pillars.title: Continuity Tax Incentives
pillars.summary: Encourage employee, family, and cooperative transitions and local headquarters/production commitment.

pillars.title: Succession Protection
pillars.summary: Planning, financing, mentoring, and estate support so firms do not vanish at retirement.

pillars.title: Procurement with Full Local Value
pillars.summary: Fair competitive purchasing that also weighs local economic and workforce impact.

pillars.title: Community Prosperity Account Link
pillars.summary: Optional resident investment in approved local enterprises under fiduciary diversification caps.

pillars.title: Proportional Reinvestment
pillars.summary: Substantial public incentives paired with transparent reinvestment commitments.

pillars.title: Cooperative Development Centers
pillars.summary: Practical legal, finance, governance, and succession support for cooperative models.

items.text: According to the National Center for Employee Ownership (NCEO) analysis of Department of Labor filings for plan year 2023, there were 6,609 ESOPs in the United States at 6,411 unique companies, covering about 15.1 million participants (about 11.0 million active) and holding over $2 trillion in total plan assets — illustrating that employee ownership is an established U.S. ownership channel, not a niche experiment.

According to USDA’s annual survey of farmer, rancher, and fishery cooperatives, there were 1,620 agricultural cooperatives in 2024 with about $275.8 billion in cooperative revenues — illustrating that member-owned cooperative enterprise remains a major channel for circulating agricultural value among producers.

local_ownership_test.purpose: Questions that keep Local Ownership design honest.
questions: Do incentives reward measured local prosperity contributions rather than punishing outside investment or firm size?
Can businesses qualify under multiple enterprise classifications without gaming?
Is the Local Prosperity Score transparent, auditable, and weighted by modeled evidence rather than political favor?
Does capital access remain fiduciary and available under published eligibility — not patronage?
Do succession tools preserve jobs and productive capacity without trapping owners into a single exit path?
Does public procurement remain competitive on price and quality while recognizing full local value?
Are Community Prosperity Account local investments capped so they complement diversified retirement savings?
Are reinvestment requirements proportional to public support and publicly reported?
